Fix an integer $n\ge0$, put $N=2^n$, and let $D_n=\{0,\ldots,N-1\}$. The big-endian encoding $\operatorname{enc}_n:\{0,1\}^n\to D_n$ is a bijection by [[thm-qc-bitstring-index-is-bijection]], so identify each address word $w$ with its slot $x=\operatorname{enc}_n(w)$. A search instance is a total Boolean function $f:D_n\to\{0,1\}$, equivalently the word-indexed function $w\mapsto f(\operatorname{enc}_n(w))$. Its marked set is $M=\{x\in D_n:f(x)=1\}$ and its marked count is $t=|M|$. The standard bit query is the coherent XOR action $U_f|x,b\rangle=|x,b\oplus f(x)\rangle$; the associated phase query is $O_M|x\rangle=(-1)^{f(x)}|x\rangle$. One standard bit query implements this phase action with a response qubit prepared in $|-\rangle$, by [[thm-qa-bit-query-to-phase-query]]. A measured candidate $x$ is verified by a separate standard bit query. Knowing $t$ is additional classical input; no count promise is made in the unknown-count version. A correct search output is a verified $x\in M$. The distinguished output none is used only by a procedure whose input includes the exact fact $t=0$; it is not a finite-time test for emptiness when $t$ is unknown.

The number $n$ may be zero, so $N=1$ and the address register then has its one-dimensional empty-word basis. The phase query is uncontrolled; no controlled-query capability is part of this definition.

For every $d\ge1$, the ordered computational basis $(e_0,\ldots,e_{d-1})$ of
the register $Q_d$ from [[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]] is an
orthonormal basis for its declared inner product. Separately, the one-dimensional
zero-qubit register has the basis $\{1\}$ by definition.

All complex inner products in this track use the root convention: they are
linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). For vectors $x,y$ in the same
space, define the Dirac pairing by

$$\langle x|y\rangle_D:=\langle y,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}.$$

The ket $|x\rangle$ denotes the vector $x$. The bra $\langle x|$ denotes the
linear functional $z\mapsto\langle z,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}$.

For finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H,K$, vectors $y\in H$ and
$x\in K$, define the rank-one linear map

$$|x\rangle\langle y|:H\to K,\qquad z\mapsto\langle z,y\rangle_{H,\mathrm{root}}x.$$

Given ordered orthonormal bases of $H$ and $K$, its coordinate matrix is
$[x][y]^\dagger$, where $[x]$ and $[y]$ are the corresponding coordinate
columns and $M^\dagger:=\overline M^{\mathsf T}$ is the conjugate transpose.
The coordinate assertion is established in
[[thm-qc-dirac-notation-coordinate-identity]].

Sine is differentiable, hence continuous, and strictly increasing on
$[-\pi/2,\pi/2]$; its endpoint values are $-1$ and $1$
([[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]],
[[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]],
[[thm-sine-cosine-signs-monotonicity-and-ranges]],
[[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]],
[[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]]). The intermediate value
theorem therefore makes its restricted image exactly $[-1,1]$
([[thm-intermediate-value]]). Likewise, cosine is continuous and strictly
decreasing on $[0,\pi]$, with endpoint values $1$ and $-1$, so its restricted
image is $[-1,1]$ ([[thm-sine-cosine-signs-monotonicity-and-ranges]],
[[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]], [[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]],
[[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[thm-intermediate-value]]).
Their principal inverses are denoted

$$\arcsin:[-1,1]\to[-\pi/2,\pi/2],\qquad\arccos:[-1,1]\to[0,\pi],$$

and are characterised by

$$\sin(\arcsin y)=y,\qquad\cos(\arccos y)=y\qquad(-1\le y\le1).$$

The chosen target intervals are part of the notation: without them, inverse
sine and inverse cosine would be multivalued relations rather than functions.
Their continuity follows from [[thm-continuous-inverse]].

Sine is strictly increasing on each interval $[-\pi/2+2m\pi,\pi/2+2m\pi]$ and strictly decreasing on each interval $[\pi/2+2m\pi,3\pi/2+2m\pi]$. Cosine is strictly decreasing on $[2m\pi,(2m+1)\pi]$ and strictly increasing on $[(2m+1)\pi,(2m+2)\pi]$. Both functions have range $[-1,1]$.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(-x)=-\sin x,\qquad\cos(-x)=\cos x,\qquad\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1.$$
Consequently $|\sin x|\le1$ and $|\cos x|\le1$.

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(x+\pi/2)=\cos x,\quad\cos(x+\pi/2)=-\sin x,\quad\sin(x+\pi)=-\sin x,\quad\cos(x+\pi)=-\cos x.$$
In particular,
$$\sin(\pi/2)=1,\quad\cos(\pi/2)=0,\quad\sin\pi=0,\quad\cos\pi=-1.$$

Let $F$ be an ordered field. For $a, b \ge 0$:

$$a < b \iff a^2 < b^2, \qquad a \le b \iff a^2 \le b^2.$$

More generally, for arbitrary $a, b \in F$, $a^2 < b^2 \iff |a| < |b|$.

derivations.claim: Orthonormality of the address basis [F2] gives $\langle G,G\rangle=t^{-1}\sum_{x,y\in M}\langle x,y\rangle=1$ and $\langle B,B\rangle=(N-t)^{-1}\sum_{x,y\notin M}\langle x,y\rangle=1$. The sets $M$ and $D_n\setminus M$ are disjoint, so every cross term in $\langle G,B\rangle$ is zero. Thus the two vectors are orthonormal.

Put $a=t/N\in(0,1)$ and $\theta=\arcsin\sqrt a$. By [F5], $\sin\theta=\sqrt a$; since $\sqrt a>0$ and $\sin0=0$ by [F9], strict increase [F6] implies $\theta>0$. Also $\sqrt a<1$ by [F11] because $a<1$, while $1=\sin(\pi/2)$ by [F10]; strict increase gives $\theta<\pi/2$ and therefore $\cos\theta>0$ by [F6]. The Pythagorean identity [F7] and square-root uniqueness [F8] give $\cos\theta=\sqrt{1-a}$. Splitting the uniform sum into $M$ and its complement now gives $|s\rangle=\sqrt{t/N}|G\rangle+\sqrt{(N-t)/N}|B\rangle =\sin\theta|G\rangle+\cos\theta|B\rangle$ and $\sin^2\theta=t/N$.

For a $T$-query quantum algorithm [[def-qa-quantum-query-algorithm]] at input length $n$, its **worst-case quantum query cost** is the maximum number of designated oracle calls over all promised instances in $P_n$ and all measurement branches. When $P_n$ is empty, define this cost to be $0$. For nonempty $P_n$, a finite circuit and finite branch sets ensure that this maximum exists; a solver whose branch counts are not uniformly bounded has infinite worst-case query cost. An expected-query bound is the separate quantity defined by [[def-qa-expected-query-cost]].

In the pure query model, ordinary gates outside the oracle calls are uncharged by the query coordinate. If a task also reports gate, preparation, measurement, or classical costs, those are separate coordinates. Bounded-error query cost uses the same worst-case maximum; its success threshold is the per-instance condition in [[def-qa-bounded-error-promise-correctness]], not an average over oracle inputs.

For every $d\ge1$, the ordered computational basis $(e_0,\ldots,e_{d-1})$ of

orthonormal basis for its declared inner product. Separately, the one-dimensional
zero-qubit register has the basis $\{1\}$ by definition.

All complex inner products in this track use the root convention: they are
linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). For vectors $x,y$ in the same

$$\langle x|y\rangle_D:=\langle y,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}.$$

The ket $|x\rangle$ denotes the vector $x$. The bra $\langle x|$ denotes the
linear functional $z\mapsto\langle z,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}$.

For finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H,K$, vectors $y\in H$ and
$x\in K$, define the rank-one linear map

$$|x\rangle\langle y|:H\to K,\qquad z\mapsto\langle z,y\rangle_{H,\mathrm{root}}x.$$

Compute the recurrence through index $m=2K+1$. For each integer $k=0,\ldots,K$, compute $p_k=(1-T_{2k+1}(q))/2$. Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

$$\lceil x\rceil\le m\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x\le m\qquad(m\in\mathbb Z).$$
For $a\ge0$, the least positive integer $n$ with $n\ge a$ is $\max\{1,\lceil a\rceil\}$. In particular $\lceil0\rceil=0$, and $\lceil k\rceil=k$ for every integer $k$.

Sine is differentiable, hence continuous, and strictly increasing on
$[-\pi/2,\pi/2]$; its endpoint values are $-1$ and $1$
([[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]],
[[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]],
[[thm-sine-cosine-signs-monotonicity-and-ranges]],
[[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]],
[[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]]). The intermediate value
theorem therefore makes its restricted image exactly $[-1,1]$
([[thm-intermediate-value]]). Likewise, cosine is continuous and strictly
decreasing on $[0,\pi]$, with endpoint values $1$ and $-1$, so its restricted
image is $[-1,1]$ ([[thm-sine-cosine-signs-monotonicity-and-ranges]],
[[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]], [[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]],
[[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[thm-intermediate-value]]).
Their principal inverses are denoted

$$\arcsin:[-1,1]\to[-\pi/2,\pi/2],\qquad\arccos:[-1,1]\to[0,\pi],$$

and are characterised by

$$\sin(\arcsin y)=y,\qquad\cos(\arccos y)=y\qquad(-1\le y\le1).$$

The chosen target intervals are part of the notation: without them, inverse
sine and inverse cosine would be multivalued relations rather than functions.
Their continuity follows from [[thm-continuous-inverse]].

$$\sin(2x)=2\sin x\cos x,\quad \cos(2x)=\cos^2x-\sin^2x=2\cos^2x-1=1-2\sin^2x,$$

$$\sin^2x=(1-\cos2x)/2,\qquad \cos^2x=(1+\cos2x)/2.$$

A claimed time bound also specifies whether it is worst-case over promised inputs and random tapes, as in [[def-probabilistic-polynomial-time-machine-interface]]. Query, nonoracle quantum gate, measurement, and classical bit costs remain distinct.

$$a < b \iff a^2 < b^2, \qquad a \le b \iff a^2 \le b^2.$$

More generally, for arbitrary $a, b \in F$, $a^2 < b^2 \iff |a| < |b|$.

derivations.claim: For $t>0$, $P(m):tm^2\ge N$ is monotone on nonnegative integers by [F9], and its least positive true index is $K=\lceil\sqrt{N/t}\rceil$ by [F2]–[F3]. The doubling loop starts with false endpoint $\mathrm{lo}=0$ and doubles $\mathrm{hi}$ until $P(\mathrm{hi})$ is true; it terminates because powers of two are unbounded. If $K=1$ it stops immediately. If $K>1$, the first true power of two satisfies $K\le\mathrm{hi}<2K$, and the preceding power $\mathrm{lo}=\mathrm{hi}/2$ is false. Upper-midpoint binary search preserves the false/true invariant and reduces each interval of width $d>1$ to width at most $\lceil d/2\rceil$, so it reaches width one after $O(\log(K+1))$ evaluations and returns the least positive true index $K$. Since $K\le\lceil\sqrt N\rceil$, the endpoints have $O(n)$ bits for $n\ge1$.

Put $a=t/N$ and $\theta=\arcsin\sqrt a$. Then $q=1-2a=\cos(2\theta)$ by [F4]–[F5]. The recurrence has base values $T_0=\cos0=1$ and $T_1=\cos(2\theta)=q$. By [F6], $$\cos(2(m+1)\theta)+\cos(2(m-1)\theta)=2\cos(2\theta)\cos(2m\theta),$$ so induction in the recurrence gives $T_m(q)=\cos(2m\theta)$ for every computed index. Therefore $p_k=(1-\cos((4k+2)\theta))/2=\sin^2((2k+1)\theta)$, and the rational list in [F1] is the actual integer-iterate success list.

Write $u=N-2t$, so $q=u/N$, and define $A_m=N^mT_m(q)$. Then $A_0=1$, $A_1=u$, and the recurrence gives $$A_{m+1}=2uA_m-N^2A_{m-1},$$ so each $A_m$ is an integer. For $n=0$, $N=t=1$, $K=1$, and all recurrence values have constant bit length.

At recurrence index $m$, multiplying the $O(mn)$-bit integer $A_m$ by the $O(n)$-bit integer $u$ costs $O(mn^2)$ schoolbook bit operations; multiplication by $N^2$ is a binary shift, and addition costs $O(mn)$. Summing over $m\le2K$ gives $O(K^2n^2)$. Each predicate evaluation in step 1.1 uses $O(n)$-bit operands and schoolbook arithmetic, hence $O(n^2)$ bit operations; the $O(\log(K+1))$ evaluations cost $O(n^2\log(K+1))\subseteq O(K^2n^2)$.

For odd $m=2k+1$, write $p_k=(N^m-A_m)/(2N^m)$. Advancing from $k-1$ to $k$ scales the previous running-best numerator by $N^2$ to put it over the new denominator, then compares the two integers and updates only on strict increase. Each comparison costs $O(Kn)$ bit operations by step 2.1, and there are $K+1$ candidates, so all comparisons cost $O(K^2n)$, within step 3.1's bound. Strict updates retain the least $k$ in a tie.

If $n=0$, necessarily $N=t=1$, so $K=1$ and the direct selection branch and finite recurrence take constant work, as stated.

**Gate model.** Use the nonoracle model of [[alg-qa-11-grover-iterate]], with exact callable $H$ and $X$ charged per occurrence and an explicitly supplied, costed exact reflection implementation. Each invoked Grover iterate retains its separate standard-bit-query and nonoracle costs.

Input $N=2^n$, exact count $t$, and standard bit-query access to $f=1_M$. If $t=0$, return none without a query. If $t>N/2$, perform at most nine independent rounds: prepare a fresh address register by $H^{\otimes n}|0^n\rangle$, measure an address, make one standard bit query to verify it, and return it if marked; after nine failures return the failure symbol.

If $0<t\le N/2$, find the least positive integer $K$ satisfying $tK^2\ge N$ by binary search. Initialize $\mathrm{lo}=0$ and $\mathrm{hi}=2^{\lceil n/2\rceil}$; while $\mathrm{hi}-\mathrm{lo}>1$, put $\mathrm{mid}=\mathrm{lo}+\lceil(\mathrm{hi}-\mathrm{lo})/2\rceil$, replace $\mathrm{hi}$ by $\mathrm{mid}$ if $t\,\mathrm{mid}^2\ge N$, and otherwise replace $\mathrm{lo}$ by $\mathrm{mid}$. Set $b$ to the least nonnegative integer with $2^b\ge K$. In each of nine independent rounds, draw $b$ fair bits to obtain $j\in\{0,\ldots,2^b-1\}$. Reject the round without a query if $j\ge K$. Otherwise prepare a fresh $|s\rangle=H^{\otimes n}|0^n\rangle$ and a fresh response qubit $|-\rangle$ using $X$ then $H$, apply [[alg-qa-11-grover-iterate]] exactly $j$ times, measure the address register, and make one separate bit query to verify the measured candidate. Return it if marked. After nine unsuccessful rounds, return the failure symbol. Uniform-state preparation uses exactly $n$ Hadamards; each iterate uses one query and a separately charged reflection. No query, state-preparation, reflection-gate, or classical-bit cost is conflated.

In the computational basis $(|0\rangle,|1\rangle)$, use $X,Y,Z$ from [[def-qc-pauli-matrices]] and define
$$H:=\frac{X+Z}{\sqrt2}=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad S:=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&i\end{pmatrix},\qquad T:=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&e^{i\pi/4}\end{pmatrix}.$$
The phases displayed in these matrices are exact; they are not identified modulo a scalar when the matrices are later placed under a control.

For real $\theta$ and a real unit vector $\mathbf n=(n_x,n_y,n_z)$, define the axis rotation
$$R_{\mathbf n}(\theta):=\exp\!\left(-\frac{i\theta}{2}\mathbf n\cdot\boldsymbol{\sigma}\right),\qquad R_z(\theta):=R_{(0,0,1)}(\theta).$$
Here $\mathbf n\cdot\boldsymbol{\sigma}$ and $\|\mathbf n\|_2$ have the meanings fixed in [[def-qc-bloch-coordinate-map]]. For a bounded endomorphism $B$ of $Q_2$, the notation $\exp(B)$ means the operator-norm series $\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}B^k/k!$ of [[lem-exponential-series-of-a-bounded-operator]] at scalar parameter $1$. Its convergence applies here because $Q_2$ is finite-dimensional and complete and every linear endomorphism of $Q_2$ is bounded ([[cor-finite-dimensional-normed-spaces-are-banach]], [[cor-linear-maps-with-finite-dimensional-domain-are-bounded]]).

The unitary identities for the fixed matrices are verified below. The following theorem proves the closed form and unitarity of each $R_{\mathbf n}(\theta)$.

Let $H$ be a finite-dimensional complex-inner-product space and let $\Pi$ be an orthogonal projection on $H$. Fix the two signs

$$R_\Pi:=2\Pi-I,\qquad S_\Pi:=I-2\Pi=-R_\Pi.$$

Thus $R_\Pi$ acts as $+I$ on $\operatorname{ran}\Pi$ and $-I$ on $\ker\Pi$; $S_\Pi$ reverses those signs. They are not interchangeable inside a controlled block. For a unit vector $\psi$, the rank-one reflection is $R_\psi=2|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|-I$ with the Dirac convention of [[def-qc-dirac-notation-conversion]].

An access model counts a direct reflection as one primitive call only when that call is explicitly declared. Controlled reflection access is a separate declaration. If $|0\rangle$ is a specified unit input in the same space $H$, the state is prepared as $\psi=U|0\rangle$ for a declared unitary $U$, and a reflection is implemented by conjugating $R_0=2|0\rangle\langle0|-I$, the construction is $UR_0U^\dagger$ and its cost must include the calls to $U$, $R_0$, and $U^\dagger$. A state vector or matrix description alone implies neither an efficient reflection nor inverse access.

Let $H$ be a finite-dimensional complex-inner-product space and let $\Pi$ be an orthogonal projection. The operators $R_\Pi=2\Pi-I$ and $S_\Pi=I-2\Pi$ are self-adjoint unitary involutions, with $R_\Pi=-S_\Pi$. On $\operatorname{ran}\Pi$ they act as $+I$ and $-I$, respectively; on $\ker\Pi$ they act as $-I$ and $+I$. In control-first order,

$$C(S_\Pi)=(Z_C)C(R_\Pi),\qquad Z_C:=\operatorname{diag}(I_H,-I_H)=Z\otimes I_H.$$

Fix a finite gate alphabet $G$ with maximum arity $k:=\max(\{r(g):g\in G\}\cup\{0\})$ and a circuit from [[def-qc-circuit-syntax-and-register-order]]. The declared **size** is the number of gate occurrences, equivalently $\sum_{t=1}^d|L_t|$; the declared **depth** is the number $d$ of explicit layers, not a minimum over alternate layerings; the **width** is the number $n$ of all wires, including workspace wires. The operation model may also assign weighted gate costs, classical bit costs, and query costs; these are separate coordinates and are summed over the calls actually made.

A workspace wire is an ancilla. A **clean-ancilla promise** specifies computational-basis zero states for the ancillas and requires their exact return for every allowed data input: if $U$ is the implemented unitary, $V_D$ is the declared data unitary, and $|0_A\rangle$ is the specified joint zero vector, then $U(x\otimes|0_A\rangle)=V_Dx\otimes|0_A\rangle$ for every allowed data vector $x$. A **dirty-ancilla promise** permits an arbitrary ancilla state independent of the data input; it may be correlated with an untouched reference. Exact dirty-ancilla restoration means the implemented unitary on data and ancillas is $V_D\otimes I_A$ on the entire joint space, where $V_D$ is the declared unitary on data. The same operator equality then holds after tensoring with the identity on any finite untouched reference. Consequently, product input between the data and the combined ancilla/reference system remains product after the operation. No uncorrelated-output claim is made for an initially data-correlated ancilla.

A controlled or inverse operation is counted only when the operation model explicitly grants that access or supplies a construction; its charge is recorded separately from an ordinary call unless the model explicitly combines them. In particular, the matrix of $U$ alone supplies neither a controlled call nor an inverse query, in accordance with [[def-qc-controlled-unitary-access]] and [[def-qc-inverse-unitary-access]].

Fix the finite circuit syntax and its complete self-delimiting binary description ([[def-qc-circuit-syntax-and-register-order]], [[def-effective-binary-encoding-and-decoder]]). For a circuit $C$, let $L(C)$ be the number of bits in that complete description, $g(C)$ its number of gate occurrences, and $w(C)$ its total number of wires.

Each clean or dirty ancilla coordinate additionally requires a declared ordered partition of the circuit wires into data register $D$ and ancilla register $A$, and a declared target unitary $V$ on $D$. In that factor order, the complete circuit unitary must satisfy the corresponding exact contract of [[def-qc-clean-and-dirty-ancillas]]. For such a supplied clean contract set $a_{\rm clean}(C)=|A|$, and for such a supplied dirty contract set $a_{\rm dirty}(C)=|A|$; the notation suppresses the declared interface, which is part of the cost instance and may differ between the two coordinates. If no corresponding contract is supplied, mark that coordinate not applicable. These are counts of declared contract registers, not maxima over possible partitions. Zero initialization alone supplies neither return contract. Every auxiliary wire remains counted in $w(C)$ ([[def-qc-elementary-circuit-resources]]).

The gate sequence and supports determine a finite dependency order: each earlier gate occurrence must precede every later occurrence that acts on a shared wire. A **layering** assigns a positive integer layer to each gate occurrence, strictly increasing along those shared-wire precedence relations. Gates in one layer therefore have pairwise disjoint supports. Define the depth $d(C)$ to be the least number of layers in such a layering; if $C$ has no gates, set $d(C)=0$. If layers are written $L_1,\ldots,L_d$ in chronological order, the denotation is $U_{L_d}\cdots U_{L_1}$, as in [[def-qc-circuit-denotational-semantics]].

For a family $(C_n)$ with a specified full-list generator $G$, let $t_G(n)$ be the worst-case number of Turing-machine transitions used by $G$ on unary input $1^n$. For a total acceptance predicate $A_n(x,z)$, let $t_A(n)$ and $s_A(n)$ be its worst-case deterministic transition count and tape-space use over all valid length-$n$ inputs and measured outputs, using a fixed effective encoding of the pair $(x,z)$. Any effective input description, classical preprocessing, or threshold computation has its own bit length and time/space bounds; these costs are not included in $t_G$ or $t_A$ unless the same machine performs them. The machine conventions are those of [[def-deterministic-one-tape-turing-machine]], [[def-partial-function-computed-by-a-machine]], and [[def-worst-case-time-and-space-complexity]].

If the access model explicitly supplies a named oracle gate $\mathcal O$, let $q_{\mathcal O}(C)$ be the number of calls to it. With several named oracles, record a separate query coordinate for each. Ordinary finite-basis gates, oracle calls, circuit-description length, generator time, and classical bit costs remain separate; no oracle, controlled-oracle, inverse-oracle, or data-loading operation is assigned zero cost unless its interface explicitly says so.

For an approximate task with declared rational tolerance $0<\epsilon<1$, let $\ell(\epsilon)$ be the bit length of that exact binary-rational encoding. Exact finite-gate computations have no precision field. The **cost record** consists of all applicable coordinates
$$\bigl(L(C_n),g(C_n),d(C_n),w(C_n),a_{\rm clean}(C_n),a_{\rm dirty}(C_n),t_G(n),t_A(n),s_A(n),q_{\mathcal O}(C_n),\epsilon,\ell(\epsilon)\bigr).$$
An inapplicable coordinate is marked not applicable, not silently charged as zero. This definition records the resource model; separate theorems establish polynomial bounds.

For $0<t<N$, let $\theta=\arcsin\sqrt{t/N}$. After an integer $k\ge0$ Grover iterates starting from $|s\rangle$, the probability of measuring a marked address is
$$p_k=\sin^2((2k+1)\theta).$$
For $t=0$ this probability is $0$, and for $t=N$ it is $1$ for every integer $k\ge0$; these endpoint cases are direct one-dimensional branches and do not normalize a nonexistent marked or unmarked state.

Sine is differentiable, hence continuous, and strictly increasing on
$[-\pi/2,\pi/2]$; its endpoint values are $-1$ and $1$
([[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]],
[[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]],
[[thm-sine-cosine-signs-monotonicity-and-ranges]],
[[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]],
[[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]]). The intermediate value
theorem therefore makes its restricted image exactly $[-1,1]$
([[thm-intermediate-value]]). Likewise, cosine is continuous and strictly
decreasing on $[0,\pi]$, with endpoint values $1$ and $-1$, so its restricted
image is $[-1,1]$ ([[thm-sine-cosine-signs-monotonicity-and-ranges]],
[[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]], [[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]],
[[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[thm-intermediate-value]]).
Their principal inverses are denoted

$$\arcsin:[-1,1]\to[-\pi/2,\pi/2],\qquad\arccos:[-1,1]\to[0,\pi],$$

and are characterised by

$$\sin(\arcsin y)=y,\qquad\cos(\arccos y)=y\qquad(-1\le y\le1).$$

The chosen target intervals are part of the notation: without them, inverse
sine and inverse cosine would be multivalued relations rather than functions.
Their continuity follows from [[thm-continuous-inverse]].

Sine is strictly increasing on each interval $[-\pi/2+2m\pi,\pi/2+2m\pi]$ and strictly decreasing on each interval $[\pi/2+2m\pi,3\pi/2+2m\pi]$. Cosine is strictly decreasing on $[2m\pi,(2m+1)\pi]$ and strictly increasing on $[(2m+1)\pi,(2m+2)\pi]$. Both functions have range $[-1,1]$.

For all real $u,v$,

$$|\sin u-\sin v|\le|u-v|,$$

and

$$|\cos u-\cos v|\le|u-v|.$$

Thus sine and cosine are Lipschitz functions on $\mathbb R$, each with
Lipschitz constant $1$.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(x+\pi/2)=\cos x,\quad\cos(x+\pi/2)=-\sin x,\quad\sin(x+\pi)=-\sin x,\quad\cos(x+\pi)=-\cos x.$$
In particular,
$$\sin(\pi/2)=1,\quad\cos(\pi/2)=0,\quad\sin\pi=0,\quad\cos\pi=-1.$$

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(2x)=2\sin x\cos x,\quad \cos(2x)=\cos^2x-\sin^2x=2\cos^2x-1=1-2\sin^2x,$$
and
$$\sin^2x=(1-\cos2x)/2,\qquad \cos^2x=(1+\cos2x)/2.$$
When defined, $\tan(2x)=2\tan x/(1-\tan^2x)$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-sine-and-cosine-addition-formulas]], [[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]], [[def-tangent-cotangent-secant-cosecant]].

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(-x)=-\sin x,\qquad\cos(-x)=\cos x,\qquad\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1.$$
Consequently $|\sin x|\le1$ and $|\cos x|\le1$.

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

Identify $\mathbb{Z}$ with its canonical copy inside $\mathbb{R}$, along the
embeddings $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Q} \to \mathbb{R}$
([[lem-nat-embeds-int]], [[lem-int-embeds-rat]], [[lem-rat-embeds-dense]],
[[def-integers]]). Then for every real $x$ there is **exactly one** integer $m$
with

$$m \;\le\; x \;<\; m + 1 .$$

It is written $\lfloor x \rfloor$ and called the **integer part**, or **floor**,
of $x$.

**Two independent ingredients are needed and neither may be dropped.** Existence
is the Archimedean property ([[thm-of-archimedean]]) together with the
well-ordering of $\mathbb{N}$ ([[thm-well-ordering-principle]]): the first says
that $x$ is caught between two integers at all, the second picks the *least*
integer above $x$. Uniqueness is the discreteness of $\mathbb{Z}$: no integer
lies strictly between $m$ and $m+1$.

This lemma is stated once here and reused. It is what turns "the nearest integer
to $x$" from a picture into an object, and the companion page's oscillator
$\psi(x) = \inf_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} |x - n|$ is computed from it in one line.

Let $\gamma$ be the unique smallest positive zero of cosine supplied by [[thm-cosine-has-a-smallest-positive-zero]]. Define
$$\pi:=2\gamma.$$

Thus $\pi>0$ and $\pi/2=\gamma$.
There is a unique $\gamma\in(0,2)$ with $\cos\gamma=0$. It is the smallest positive zero of cosine.

Identify integers and naturals with their canonical copies in the reals. For every real $x$, put $\lceil x\rceil=-\lfloor-x\rfloor$, using [[lem-integer-part]]. Then $\lceil x\rceil$ is an integer, $x\le\lceil x\rceil$, and
$$\lceil x\rceil\le m\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x\le m\qquad(m\in\mathbb Z).$$
For $a\ge0$, the least positive integer $n$ with $n\ge a$ is $\max\{1,\lceil a\rceil\}$. In particular $\lceil0\rceil=0$, and $\lceil k\rceil=k$ for every integer $k$.

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with

Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

$$a < b \iff a^2 < b^2, \qquad a \le b \iff a^2 \le b^2.$$

More generally, for arbitrary $a, b \in F$, $a^2 < b^2 \iff |a| < |b|$.

**Gate model.** Use the nonoracle model of [[alg-qa-11-grover-iterate]], with exact callable $H$ and $X$ charged per occurrence and an explicitly supplied, costed exact reflection implementation. Each invoked Grover iterate retains its separate standard-bit-query and nonoracle costs.

Input $N=2^n$ and standard bit-query access to $f=1_M$, with no input giving $t=|M|$. Fix $c=3/2$ and initialize $\ell=0$. In each round increment $\ell$ and put $M_\ell=\lceil c^\ell\rceil$. First draw one uniform address $x\in D_n$ and verify it by one standard bit query; if $f(x)=1$, return $x$. Otherwise choose $j$ uniformly from $\{1,\ldots,M_\ell\}$, prepare a fresh address register as $|s\rangle=H^{\otimes n}|0^n\rangle$ and a fresh response qubit as $|-\rangle$ using $X$ then $H$, apply the Grover iterate exactly $j$ times, measure the address register, and verify the candidate by a separate standard bit query. Return a verified marked item and otherwise begin the next round. Every random choice and quantum register is fresh in each round. The algorithm has no false positive; when $t=0$ it continues forever and does not produce a finite-time emptiness decision. The gate and state-preparation costs are charged separately from the bit-query count.

Fix an integer $n\ge0$, put $N=2^n$, and let $D_n=\{0,\ldots,N-1\}$. The big-endian encoding $\operatorname{enc}_n:\{0,1\}^n\to D_n$ is a bijection by [[thm-qc-bitstring-index-is-bijection]], so identify each address word $w$ with its slot $x=\operatorname{enc}_n(w)$. A search instance is a total Boolean function $f:D_n\to\{0,1\}$, equivalently the word-indexed function $w\mapsto f(\operatorname{enc}_n(w))$. Its marked set is $M=\{x\in D_n:f(x)=1\}$ and its marked count is $t=|M|$. The standard bit query is the coherent XOR action $U_f|x,b\rangle=|x,b\oplus f(x)\rangle$; the associated phase query is $O_M|x\rangle=(-1)^{f(x)}|x\rangle$. One standard bit query implements this phase action with a response qubit prepared in $|-\rangle$, by [[thm-qa-bit-query-to-phase-query]]. A measured candidate $x$ is verified by a separate standard bit query. Knowing $t$ is additional classical input; no count promise is made in the unknown-count version. A correct search output is a verified $x\in M$. The distinguished output none is used only by a procedure whose input includes the exact fact $t=0$; it is not a finite-time test for emptiness when $t$ is unknown.

The number $n$ may be zero, so $N=1$ and the address register then has its one-dimensional empty-word basis. The phase query is uncontrolled; no controlled-query capability is part of this definition.

Let $0<a=t/N<3/4$, $\theta=\arcsin\sqrt a$, and let $J$ be uniform on $\{1,\ldots,M\}$. If the positive integer $M$ satisfies $M\ge4/\sqrt a$, then
$$\mathbb E[\sin^2((2J+1)\theta)]\ge\frac38.$$

If $0<a<3/4$, the schedule $M_\ell=\lceil(3/2)^\ell\rceil$ tends to infinity, so some finite $L$ satisfies $M_L\ge4/\sqrt a$. Input $N=2^n$, standard bit-query access to $f=1_M$, and the exact integer $t=|M|$. If $t=0$, return none without a query. Thus $K=\mathrm{hi}=\lceil\sqrt{N/t}\rceil$. Prepare $|s\rangle=H^{\otimes n}|0^n\rangle$, set $q=1-2t/N$, and compute exactly the rational recurrence
$$T_0(q)=1,\qquad T_1(q)=q,\qquad T_{m+1}(q)=2qT_m(q)-T_{m-1}(q)\quad(1\le m\le2K).$$
Compute the recurrence through index $m=2K+1$. For each integer $k=0,\ldots,K$, compute $p_k=(1-T_{2k+1}(q))/2$. Choose the least $k$ attaining the maximum of this finite rational list, apply [[alg-qa-11-grover-iterate]] exactly $k$ times, measure the address register, and make one separate standard bit query to verify the candidate. Return the candidate if marked and the failure symbol otherwise. The state preparation, all-zero reflection, classical recurrence and comparison work, and oracle queries are distinct costs; this definition makes no polynomial-time preprocessing claim.

For $0<t<N$, let $\theta=\arcsin\sqrt{t/N}$. After an integer $k\ge0$ Grover iterates starting from $|s\rangle$, the probability of measuring a marked address is
$$p_k=\sin^2((2k+1)\theta).$$
For $t=0$ this probability is $0$, and for $t=N$ it is $1$ for every integer $k\ge0$; these endpoint cases are direct one-dimensional branches and do not normalize a nonexistent marked or unmarked state.

Put $a=t/N$ and $\theta=\arcsin\sqrt a$. If $0<a\le1/2$, some integer $k$ with $0\le k\le K=\lceil1/\sqrt a\rceil$ has
$$p_k=\sin^2((2k+1)\theta)\ge1-a.$$
If $1/2<a\le1$, $k=0$ lies in this range and $p_0=a>1/2$. The real-valued optimizer $k_*=\pi/(4\theta)-1/2$ is not in general an integer.

Let $0<a=t/N<3/4$, $\theta=\arcsin\sqrt a$, and let $J$ be uniform on $\{1,\ldots,M\}$. If the positive integer $M$ satisfies $M\ge4/\sqrt a$, then
$$\mathbb E[\sin^2((2J+1)\theta)]\ge\frac38.$$

For $t>0$, the BBHT algorithm halts with probability $1$ and returns an element of $M$; the probability it has not returned a marked item after $r$ rounds tends to zero. For $t=0$, it never halts and never outputs an element.

One execution of [[alg-qa-11-grover-iterate]] makes exactly one standard bit-query call, through phase kickback. The response-qubit preparation and the reflection about $|s\rangle$ make no oracle calls and are charged separately as gates or explicitly supplied reflection operations.

Fix a promised input $z$ and a sequential procedure whose elementary steps are deterministic transitions, finite random transitions, finite-outcome measurements, or a single oracle call. At every live history, the next transition has a specified probability law on a finite outcome set; a query step has one successor and issues one call. A halted history is extended by deterministic idle steps that issue no calls.

For $M\in\mathbb N$, let $\Omega_M$ be the finite set of length-$M$ histories with the recursively assigned transition weights. Let $C_M:\Omega_M\to\{0,\ldots,M\}$ count the oracle calls actually executed in those $M$ steps. Define the **expected query cost** on input $z$ by
$$
\mathbb E_{\mathrm{query}}(z):=\sup_{M\in\mathbb N}\mathbb E[C_M]\in[0,\infty],
$$
where each expectation is taken on the finite probability space of the corresponding prefix. Define the pathwise total query count on an infinite history $\omega$ by $C(\omega):=\sup_M C_M(\omega)$. No probability measure or expectation of $C$ on an infinite history space is presumed by this definition.

If a procedure is organized into rounds, each padded to at most $K$ elementary steps for some fixed integer $K\ge1$ and containing at most one query, its first $R$ rounds are the prefix of length $KR$. Hence the supremum of its finite-round expected query counts equals the displayed finite-step supremum. In particular, query-indexed rounds are valid when each round contains exactly one query, as in Simon sampling.

$$\lceil x\rceil\le m\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x\le m\qquad(m\in\mathbb Z).$$
For $a\ge0$, the least positive integer $n$ with $n\ge a$ is $\max\{1,\lceil a\rceil\}$. In particular $\lceil0\rceil=0$, and $\lceil k\rceil=k$ for every integer $k$.

nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field. For $a, b \ge 0$:

$$a < b \iff a^2 < b^2, \qquad a \le b \iff a^2 \le b^2.$$

More generally, for arbitrary $a, b \in F$, $a^2 < b^2 \iff |a| < |b|$.

An expected-query bound is the separate quantity defined by [[def-qa-expected-query-cost]].

If a task also reports gate, preparation, measurement, or classical costs, those are separate coordinates. First suppose $a\ge3/4$. Each round succeeds at least on its direct uniform sample, with probability at least $3/4$ by [F1]. The probability of reaching round $\ell$ is at most $(1/4)^{\ell-1}$. It is an absolute constant, hence $O(1/\sqrt a)$ by [F7].

Before stage $L$, bound every reach probability by $1$. The geometric sum of $(3/2)^\ell$ over $\ell<L$ is at most $3(3/2)^{L-1}<12/\sqrt a$, while the additive $3$ per round contributes $3(L-1)=O(1/\sqrt a)$ by step 1.2. Thus the early-stage expected query count is $O(1/\sqrt a)$.

Since $$M_{L+k}\le(3/2)^kM_L+1,$$ the tail expected query count is at most $$\sum_{k\ge0}(5/8)^k((3/2)^kM_L+3),$$ which is $16M_L+8=O(1/\sqrt a)$ because $(5/8)(3/2)=15/16<1$, $M_L\le7/\sqrt a$ by step 1.2, and $8=O(1/\sqrt a)$ by [F7].

[[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]], [[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]],

$$\arcsin:[-1,1]\to[-\pi/2,\pi/2],\qquad\arccos:[-1,1]\to[0,\pi],$$

$$\sin(\arcsin y)=y,\qquad\cos(\arccos y)=y\qquad(-1\le y\le1).$$

For $0<t<N$, let $\theta=\arcsin\sqrt{t/N}$. After an integer $k\ge0$ Grover iterates starting from $|s\rangle$, the probability of measuring a marked address is
$$p_k=\sin^2((2k+1)\theta).$$
For $t=0$ this probability is $0$, and for $t=N$ it is $1$ for every integer $k\ge0$; these endpoint cases are direct one-dimensional branches and do not normalize a nonexistent marked or unmarked state.

Sine is differentiable, hence continuous, and strictly increasing on
$[-\pi/2,\pi/2]$; its endpoint values are $-1$ and $1$
([[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]],
[[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]],
[[thm-sine-cosine-signs-monotonicity-and-ranges]],
[[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]],
[[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]]). The intermediate value
theorem therefore makes its restricted image exactly $[-1,1]$
([[thm-intermediate-value]]). Likewise, cosine is continuous and strictly
decreasing on $[0,\pi]$, with endpoint values $1$ and $-1$, so its restricted
image is $[-1,1]$ ([[thm-sine-cosine-signs-monotonicity-and-ranges]],
[[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]], [[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]],
[[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[thm-intermediate-value]]).
Their principal inverses are denoted

$$\arcsin:[-1,1]\to[-\pi/2,\pi/2],\qquad\arccos:[-1,1]\to[0,\pi],$$

and are characterised by

$$\sin(\arcsin y)=y,\qquad\cos(\arccos y)=y\qquad(-1\le y\le1).$$

The chosen target intervals are part of the notation: without them, inverse
sine and inverse cosine would be multivalued relations rather than functions.
Their continuity follows from [[thm-continuous-inverse]].

Sine is strictly increasing on each interval $[-\pi/2+2m\pi,\pi/2+2m\pi]$ and strictly decreasing on each interval $[\pi/2+2m\pi,3\pi/2+2m\pi]$. Cosine is strictly decreasing on $[2m\pi,(2m+1)\pi]$ and strictly increasing on $[(2m+1)\pi,(2m+2)\pi]$. Both functions have range $[-1,1]$.

Let $\gamma$ be the unique smallest positive zero of cosine supplied by [[thm-cosine-has-a-smallest-positive-zero]]. Define
$$\pi:=2\gamma.$$

Thus $\pi>0$ and $\pi/2=\gamma$.
There is a unique $\gamma\in(0,2)$ with $\cos\gamma=0$. It is the smallest positive zero of cosine.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(x+\pi/2)=\cos x,\quad\cos(x+\pi/2)=-\sin x,\quad\sin(x+\pi)=-\sin x,\quad\cos(x+\pi)=-\cos x.$$
In particular,
$$\sin(\pi/2)=1,\quad\cos(\pi/2)=0,\quad\sin\pi=0,\quad\cos\pi=-1.$$

For all real $x,y$,
$$\sin(x+y)=\sin x\cos y+\cos x\sin y,$$
$$\cos(x+y)=\cos x\cos y-\sin x\sin y.$$

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(2x)=2\sin x\cos x,\quad \cos(2x)=\cos^2x-\sin^2x=2\cos^2x-1=1-2\sin^2x,$$
and
$$\sin^2x=(1-\cos2x)/2,\qquad \cos^2x=(1+\cos2x)/2.$$
When defined, $\tan(2x)=2\tan x/(1-\tan^2x)$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-sine-and-cosine-addition-formulas]], [[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]], [[def-tangent-cotangent-secant-cosecant]].

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

derivations.claim: Put $x=\pi/4$, $s=\sin x$, and $c=\cos x$. Since $0<\pi/4<\pi/2$ by [F4], [F3] gives $s,c>0$. By [F7] and [F5], $0=\cos(\pi/2)=\cos(2x)=c^2-s^2$, so $(c-s)(c+s)=0$. Since $c+s>0$, we have $c=s$. Then [F7] and [F5] give $1=\sin(\pi/2)=\sin(2x)=2sc=2s^2$, so [F9] gives $s=1/\sqrt2$. Thus $\arcsin(1/\sqrt2)=\pi/4$ by [F2], and $k_*=\pi/(4(\pi/4))-1/2=1/2$.

The legal standard query counts are integers, so $k_*=1/2$ is not executable. Applying the integer formula [F1] gives $p_0=\sin^2(\pi/4)=1/2$ and $p_1=\sin^2(3\pi/4)=1/2$, whereas substituting the noninteger $k_*$ into the trigonometric expression would give $\sin^2(\pi/2)=1$. The continuous expression therefore does not describe an allowed standard Grover circuit at this input.
